name: circular-list?
summary: #t if following the cdrs of x eventually arrives back somewhere it has already been.
explanation: A list is a chain of pairs, and nothing stops the last cdr from pointing back into the chain instead of at the empty list. Such a list has no end: walking it never terminates, and length, map, append and for-each all run forever on it. circular-list? is the verb that asks the question safely, using two cursors that advance at different speeds -- if the fast one ever lands on the same pair as the slow one there must be a cycle, and if it runs off the end there is not. Together with proper-list? and dotted-list? it partitions every value in the language into exactly three cases: ends in (), ends in a non-pair, or never ends. Every value is in exactly one of them, which is what makes the three predicates worth learning as a set rather than one at a time. In practice circular-list? is a guard: you call it on input you did not construct, before you hand that input to a verb that assumes an end exists. It never mutates and never allocates, and it costs at most a linear walk.

examples.note: (#f #t) -- an ordinary list is not circular; one built by circular-list is.
(empty #f proper #f dotted #f atom #f circular #t) -- only a genuine cycle answers #t; everything else, including non-lists, answers #f.
(proper proper dotted dotted circular) -- the three predicates partition every value, so the cond needs no else-case beyond the third.

caveats: A circular list cannot be displayed. Printing one walks it forever; the engine fails rather than returning. Test it, branch on it, but do not hand it to display.
Nearly every list verb loops forever on a circular list: length, map, append, for-each, reverse. length+ is the exception that reports #f instead.
#f does not mean 'proper list'. A dotted pair, a number and a string all answer #f. Use proper-list? when you mean proper.
It only follows CDRs. A list whose car points back at the list itself is not circular by this definition, and it will still hang anything that recurses into cars.

circular-list is the only ordinary way to build one; the other way is set-cdr! on a pair you already hold. If you never do either, the predicate always answers #f and the guard costs a walk for nothing.
usecases: Guarding a recursive list walk against input that arrived from outside the program.
Classifying a value's shape alongside proper-list? and dotted-list?, where the three cases are exhaustive.
Deciding whether to use length or length+ before measuring something you did not build.

learn.concept: The three list-shape predicates partition every value, and the reason there are three is that a chain of pairs can end in (), end in something else, or not end.
learn.progression: Ask it about an ordinary list and get #f, which teaches nothing. Build one with circular-list, ask again, and then try to display it -- the failure is the lesson. Then write the three-way shape classifier and notice the cond is exhaustive with no fallback.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (accept-payload x)
  (cond ((circular-list? x) (list 'reject 'cyclic))
        ((not (proper-list? x)) (list 'reject 'malformed))
        ((null? x) (list 'accept 0))
        (else (list 'accept (length x)))))
(display (list (accept-payload '(a b c)) (accept-payload '()) (accept-payload '(a . b)) (accept-payload (circular-list 'a 'b))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define c (circular-list 'a 'b))
(display (list 'circular-says (circular-list? c)
               'proper-says (proper-list? c)
               'dotted-says (dotted-list? c)
               'length+-says (length+ c)
               'pair-says (pair? c)))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A service receives a list from a caller it does not trust and must decide whether to process it. Candidates: circular-list? (one bounded walk, answers the exact question 'will iterating this terminate', and the rejection has a reason), list? (asks a different question -- in R7RS it is required to terminate on circular input, but a #f answer does not tell you WHICH failure it was), length+ (also cycle-safe and gives the size too, but conflates 'circular' with a #f you then have to interpret), a depth counter with a cap (rejects long-but-valid input and the cap is arbitrary), doing nothing and letting length hang (the service stops responding with nothing in the log). circular-list? is the pick when the rejection reason has to be reportable.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: an admission check with a distinct rejection reason for cyclic and for malformed, because a caller can fix one and probably cannot fix the other. math: the same predicate read as 'does following this chain terminate', across all five shapes a value can have. cs: all five predicates asked about the SAME circular list, which is the only way to see that circular-list? is the only one that says yes, that proper-list? and dotted-list? both say no, and that pair? cheerfully says yes because a cycle is still made of pairs.
row-2-audit.meta: Why circular-list? and not just length+: length+ answers #f for a cycle and a number otherwise, so it can serve as a guard. But it reads as a measurement, and a reader has to know the #f convention to see the guard. Naming the check is the point.
row-2-audit.eng: A rejection reason a caller can act on is worth more than a boolean. 'Cyclic' tells them their serialiser is wrong; 'malformed' tells them their input is truncated.
row-2-audit.math: Termination is a property of the structure, not of the algorithm. A cycle makes every unbounded traversal diverge, no matter what it was computing.
row-2-audit.cs: pair? answering #t on a circular list is the honest reminder that these predicates ask about SHAPE, not about type. It is still a pair; it just has no end.

row-3-dimension.setup: Asking whether following a chain of references gets you out, or gets you back to where you started.

rungs.domain: a conveyor of station hand-offs, where a loop means product never leaves the line
rungs.code:
(define (line-terminates? route)
  (if (circular-list? route) 'never-exits 'exits))
(define straight (list 'intake 'weld 'paint 'crate))
(define looped (circular-list 'intake 'weld 'inspect))
(display (list 'straight (line-terminates? straight)
               'stations (length straight)
               'looped (line-terminates? looped)
               'measurable (length+ looped)))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a garbage collector or serialiser deciding whether a structure can be written out at all
rungs.code:
(define (writable? x)
  (cond ((circular-list? x) (list 'no 'would-not-terminate))
        ((proper-list? x) (list 'yes (length x)))
        (else (list 'yes 'atom-or-dotted))))
(define graph (list 'a 'b 'c))
(define cyclic-graph (circular-list 'a 'b))
(display (list 'graph (writable? graph)
               'cyclic (writable? cyclic-graph)
               'dotted (writable? '(a . b))))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: Bare, it is a yes-or-no about three chains and there is nothing at stake. On a production line the same question becomes whether product ever leaves: a route that loops back is not slow, it is unfinishable, and the honest report is that the length is not merely large but undefined. For a serialiser the question becomes whether the structure can be written down at all -- and the answer 'no, it would not terminate' is a different refusal from 'no, it is too big', which is why the reason travels with the verdict. Same predicate throughout; what climbs is what non-termination COSTS -- nothing, then a line that never delivers, then a writer that never returns.
row-3-dimension.meta: The ladder is about the consequence of the #t answer. It is the rare predicate whose false case is boring everywhere and whose true case gets steadily more expensive, which is exactly why it is worth calling before you need it.
row-3-dimension.eng: A routing loop is not a performance problem. It is a correctness problem that presents as a performance problem, which is why it takes so long to find.
row-3-dimension.math: A path that revisits a node has no length. Asking for one is not asking a hard question, it is asking a question with no answer.
row-3-dimension.cs: Every serialiser eventually grows cycle detection, and the ones that grow it after shipping learn about it from a hung process rather than from a test.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (exactly-one-shape? x)
  (= 1 (length (filter (lambda (b) b)
                       (list (circular-list? x) (proper-list? x) (dotted-list? x))))))
(display (map exactly-one-shape?
              (list '() '(1 2 3) '(1 . 2) 42 (circular-list 1 2))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (built-cycles-are-detected? n)
  (let ((c (apply circular-list (list-tabulate n (lambda (i) i)))))
    (and (circular-list? c) (pair? c) (not (proper-list? c)))))
(display (map built-cycles-are-detected? '(1 2 3 5 8)))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: Every value is in exactly one of the three shape classes -- circular, proper, or dotted; a list is circular if and only if length+ cannot measure it; and every list built by circular-list is detected as circular no matter how many elements it has, including one.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all x. exactly one of circular-list?(x), proper-list?(x), dotted-list?(x) holds; circular-list?(x) iff length+(x) = #f; and for all n >= 1. circular-list?(apply circular-list (0..n-1))
row-4-proof.meta: The first claim is the strong one, because it is what licenses the three-way cond with no fallback -- and it is checked on all five shapes including a bare number. The second ties the predicate to the measurement verb so the two can never drift. The third is the constructor round-trip, and the one-element case is there because a single pair whose cdr points at itself is the smallest cycle and the one a two-cursor walk is most likely to get wrong.
row-4-proof.eng: An exhaustive partition is what lets a classifier be written as a cond with no default arm. A default arm is where unclassified inputs go to be mishandled quietly.
row-4-proof.math: Exactly-one is stronger than at-least-one and stronger than at-most-one, and both halves have to be checked. A test that only confirmed one predicate fires would miss an overlap.
row-4-proof.cs: A cycle of length one is the degenerate case for Floyd's two-cursor walk, because the fast and slow cursors are already equal after a single step.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (safe? x) (not (circular-list? x)))
(define (process-batch items)
  (let ((usable (filter safe? items)))
    (list 'received (length items)
          'usable (length usable)
          'rejected (- (length items) (length usable))
          'total-elements (apply + (map length usable)))))
(display (process-batch (list '(1 2) (circular-list 'x) '(3 4 5) '() (circular-list 'y 'z))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (finite? x) (not (circular-list? x)))
(define (total-cardinality sets)
  (if (every finite? sets)
      (apply + (map length sets))
      'unbounded))
(display (list 'all-finite (total-cardinality (list '(a b) '(c) '()))
               'one-infinite (total-cardinality (list '(a b) (circular-list 'c)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (cyclic? x) (circular-list? x))
(define (audit structures)
  (fold (lambda (s acc)
          (cond ((cyclic? s) (list (car acc) (cadr acc) (+ 1 (caddr acc))))
                ((proper-list? s) (list (+ 1 (car acc)) (cadr acc) (caddr acc)))
                (else (list (car acc) (+ 1 (cadr acc)) (caddr acc)))))
        (list 0 0 0)
        structures))
(display (list 'proper-dotted-circular
               (audit (list '(1 2) '(1 . 2) (circular-list 'a) '() 7 (circular-list 'b 'c)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: circular-list? answers whether a chain of pairs ever ends.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: safe? is one call; process-batch filters a whole batch through it and then aggregates only what survived -- the total element count is computable precisely because the unmeasurable inputs were removed first, and the rejection count is reported rather than hidden. math: finite? is one call; total-cardinality uses every to require ALL parts finite before summing, because one infinite part makes the total unbounded regardless of the others. cs: cyclic? is one call; audit folds the three-way classification across a heterogeneous pile and returns a census, turning a predicate into a profile of a whole data set.
row-5-emergence.meta: The composition is always guard-then-aggregate, and the interesting decision is what an unsafe element does to the aggregate. Filtering it out (eng) reports a partial total; requiring all-safe (math) refuses to report at all; counting it (cs) makes it part of the answer. Those are three genuinely different policies and the base predicate makes all three expressible.
row-5-emergence.eng: Reporting how many were rejected alongside the total is what stops a filtered aggregate from being read as a complete one.
row-5-emergence.math: The sum of cardinalities is defined only when every summand is finite. Checking that first is not defensive programming, it is the precondition.
row-5-emergence.cs: A shape census over a data set is the cheapest way to find out that the one structure you did not expect is in there, and it costs one bounded walk per item.
